At room temperature in compression, the binary Fe-26Al stress–strain curve consists of a linear elastic part followed by a parabolic hardening stage (Fig. 2b); in tension it fails in a brittle manner (Fig. 3b).

Fe-26Al exhibits tension–compression asymmetry: yield stress in compression (644 MPa) is higher than in tension (475 MPa); the text states that the tension–compression asymmetry of Fe-26Al-based alloys is higher than that of Fe-15Al-based alloys.

At 650 °C the binary Fe-26Al yield-stress bars stay close to the 100 MPa tick and are the shortest among Fe-26Al-based alloys (Fig. 7); at 800 °C Fe-26Al shows the smallest yield stress (Fig. 8); no numeric value labels are printed on the bars.

In the elevated-temperature compression curves, binary Fe-26Al is strongest at room temperature (above the 600 MPa gridline) but weakest above ~600 °C, dropping to the 0–50 MPa range at 800 °C (Fig. 6).
Fracture surface of Fe-26Al after room-temperature tensile testing: very coarse transgranular fracture with a large smooth facet crossing the field (Fig. 4f); fracture mode TGC.
